Predicting Cardiovascular Disease Risk From Health Survey Data

Sammy Dandu

Introduction¶

Cardiovascular disease remains one of the leading causes of illness and death worldwide, and its impact extends far beyond the hospital. It affects families through sudden events like heart attacks and strokes, and it affects communities through long-term disability, reduced quality of life, and high healthcare costs. What makes cardiovascular disease especially important from a prevention perspective is that many contributing factors develop gradually over years. Conditions such as diabetes, obesity, depression, and lifestyle patterns like smoking and low physical activity often appear well before a major cardiac event occurs. This means that identifying higher-risk individuals earlier, even before symptoms are severe, can create opportunities for better screening, targeted prevention strategies, and timely clinical follow-up.

Among prevention efforts, there are broad public health guidelines that target the general population, and there are more targeted strategies that focus on individuals who are most at risk. Targeted prevention is appealing because it can help allocate limited resources more effectively. Instead of applying the same level of attention to everyone, healthcare providers and public health agencies can prioritize education, screening, and support for the groups that are most likely to benefit. Doing this well requires more than intuition. It requires evidence that helps quantify which combinations of risk factors are most strongly associated with heart disease and how those factors interact across different groups.

This is where data science becomes useful. Large health survey datasets capture many of the inputs related to cardiovascular risk, including demographics, lifestyle behaviors, and medical history. By analyzing these variables, we can estimate how heart disease prevalence changes across different groups and build predictive models that identify patterns too complex to evaluate by hand. In practice, data science turns a set of measured factors into a structured risk estimate that can support decision making. This does not replace a clinician, but it can help highlight who may need closer attention and which factors tend to carry the most signal in the data.

In this tutorial, we walk through a complete data science pipeline for cardiovascular disease risk prediction using health survey data. We start by curating and preparing the dataset so that categorical variables are properly encoded and numeric variables are in a usable form. Next, we perform exploratory data analysis focused on prevalence rather than raw counts, which is especially important because heart disease is relatively rare in the dataset. We then move into feature selection to identify which variables are most informative, and we train and evaluate machine learning models using metrics that are appropriate for imbalanced outcomes. Finally, we summarize what the analysis suggests and discuss how these results can be interpreted responsibly as predictive insight rather than proof of causation.

However, there are important constraints and limitations to keep in mind. Survey data may include self reported answers, which can introduce measurement error, and some variables may act as proxies for other factors such as age or overall health burden. In addition, a predictive model can only learn patterns present in the dataset and does not automatically generalize to every population or clinical setting. The goal of this tutorial is not to build a medical diagnostic tool, but to guide the reader through how to apply the data science lifecycle to a high impact healthcare problem and to show how careful analysis can produce useful, interpretable insights.

Data Collection¶

The dataset used in this project comes from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS). BRFSS is the nation’s premier system of health related telephone surveys, designed to collect state level data on U.S. residents. Through these surveys, BRFSS gathers information on topics such as health related risk behaviors, chronic health conditions, and the use of preventive services. Because it is conducted across states and captures a wide range of health and lifestyle factors, BRFSS provides a large and practical dataset for studying patterns related to cardiovascular disease risk.

The code below loads the BRFSS heart disease dataset into a Pandas DataFrame. First, it imports the core libraries we’ll use throughout the tutorial. Next, it reads the CSV file into a DataFrame, and then prints the first few rows out so we can quickly verify that the data loaded correctly and preview the columns and example values before starting preprocessing and analysis.

Data Pre-Processing and Exploratory Data Analysis¶

We start by running df.info() to get a quick health check of the dataset. This tells us how many rows and columns we have, which columns are numeric vs. categorical, and whether there are any missing values. We do this because machine learning models require clean, consistent inputs, and this step helps us spot what needs to be converted before we can train anything.

Next, we generate a small summary table of the categorical columns. For each categorical feature, we list how many unique values it has and show the actual category labels. We do this so we can decide the correct encoding strategy: columns with only two values (like Yes/No) can be converted to 0 and 1, while columns with many categories (like Age_Category or General_Health) should be handled with one-hot encoding. This step prevents us from guessing and ensures our preprocessing choices match what is actually in the data.

EDA #1¶

The plots below summarize the distribution of key categorical variables in the dataset and show that most features have reasonable coverage across categories, with a few categories being relatively rare. For General_Health, responses are concentrated in the more positive categories: Very Good (35.9%) and Good (30.5%) make up the majority, followed by Excellent (18.3%), while Fair (11.6%) and especially Poor (3.7%) represent smaller portions of the sample. This is helpful context for interpretation because “Poor” and “Fair” are less common but, as shown earlier, they correspond to much higher heart disease prevalence. For Checkup, most respondents report recent healthcare utilization, with 78.1% having a checkup within the past year, while the remaining categories are much smaller (11.5% within the past 2 years, 5.5% within the past 5 years, 4.5% 5+ years ago, and only 0.5% reporting “Never”). For the binary variables, the sample is generally well-populated on both sides: Exercise is skewed toward “Yes” (77.2%) versus “No” (22.8%), Smoking_History shows a substantial minority reporting “Yes” (40.6%) versus “No” (59.4%), Depression is reported by about 20.0% of respondents, and Arthritis is fairly common (32.7%). Both Skin_Cancer and Other_Cancer are relatively rare at about 9.7% each, meaning they are still usable as predictors but may behave more like “comorbidity indicators” than broadly distributed lifestyle factors. Sex is close to balanced (51.9% Female, 48.1% Male), and the Age_Category distribution is spread across all groups but is weighted more heavily toward middle-to-older ages (for example, several of the largest bins appear in the 50–74 range), which aligns with the overall heart disease prevalence being non-trivial in this dataset.

After that, we are now ready to convert all of the non-numeric survey responses into machine-learning-ready numeric features.

First, we define mapping dictionaries to turn simple two-category fields into numbers. For columns like Arthritis, Depression, Exercise, Heart_Disease, Skin_Cancer, etc., we convert No → 0 and Yes → 1. We do the same for Sex by mapping Female → 0 and Male → 1. Before applying the mappings, we strip whitespace from the text values (e.g., turning " Yes" into "Yes") so we don’t accidentally create “fake” categories caused by inconsistent formatting.

Next, we handle Diabetes, which originally has multiple categories. Here, we collapse it into a binary risk-factor indicator by mapping No and No, pre-diabetes or borderline diabetes to 0, and mapping Yes (including pregnancy-only diabetes) to 1. We do this to simplify the feature into a clean diabetes present vs. not present variable, which is easier to interpret and model as a risk factor.

Finally, we apply one-hot encoding to multi-category columns (Checkup, General_Health, Age_Category) using pd.get_dummies(). This creates a separate 0/1 column for each category, which prevents the model from incorrectly treating the categories as numeric magnitudes. We then re-run df.info() to confirm the transformation worked (you’ll see more columns now, and many former object columns converted into numeric/boolean types).

In [217]:
# This cell converts binary categorical columns into numeric 0/1 values.
# We map "No"->0 and "Yes"->1 for health-condition style fields, and "Female"->0, "Male"->1 for Sex,
# so these variables can be directly used by ML models without one-hot encoding.

binary_map = {"No": 0, "Yes": 1}
binary_sex_map = {"Female": 0, "Male": 1}

binary_cols = [
    "Arthritis",
    "Depression",
    "Exercise",
    "Heart_Disease",
    "Other_Cancer",
    "Skin_Cancer",
    "Smoking_History"
]
sex_col = "Sex"

# Clean whitespace just in case (prevents " Yes" vs "Yes" issues)
for c in binary_cols + [sex_col]:
    df[c] = df[c].astype(str).str.strip()

# Apply mappings
df[binary_cols] = df[binary_cols].replace(binary_map)
df[sex_col] = df[sex_col].replace(binary_sex_map)

Next, we need to check and see whether our target variable (Heart_Disease) is balanced or imbalanced, and then visualize it.

First, we compute the counts of each class (0 = No, 1 = Yes) using value_counts().sort_index(), so the bars appear in a consistent order (0 then 1). Next, we convert those counts into percentages by dividing each count by the total number of rows and multiplying by 100.

Then we create a bar chart of the raw counts, but we annotate each bar with the corresponding percentage (e.g., ~91.8% for class 0 and ~8.2% for class 1). We do this because the count plot shows the scale of the dataset, while the percentages clearly show the degree of class imbalance.

This step is important because a heavily imbalanced target can make accuracy misleading (a model can look “good” by mostly predicting the majority class). Knowing this early helps us choose better evaluation metrics later (like precision/recall, F1, ROC-AUC/PR-AUC) and consider imbalance-aware modeling strategies if needed.

Now, we need to make sure that we're completely ready to move onto feature selection. As such, we take every column that is currently stored as a boolean (True/False) and convert it into an integer (1/0). This is mostly for convenience and compatibility, as many ML workflows (and some metrics, correlations, or feature selection routines) behave more consistently when all features are numeric types instead of mixed boolean and numeric dtypes. Conceptually, nothing about the information changes, you are just representing the same one hot flags in a standard numeric form.

Second, we need to check for missing values by computing df.isna().sum() for every column, sorting them, and displaying the top 10. The output shows zeros across the board, which means there are no NaN values in your dataset at this point. That is a good sign because it means we do not need an imputation step (like filling missing values with medians, means, or a special category) before training models.

Finally, df.info() confirms the dataset’s structure after all of this processing. The dtypes are now fully numeric: 7 columns are float64 (your continuous variables like height, weight, BMI, and consumption measures) and the remaining 32 columns are int64 (binary variables and one hot encoded category indicators). The key takeaway is that your dataset is now “model ready” in the sense that everything is numeric and complete, so you can safely train ML models without extra preprocessing for missing data or categorical handling.

These are some functions I created to make EDA a little easier to visualize:

In [225]:
# Since Heart_Disease is Rare (~8%), we Focus on Prevalence (%), or How Common Heart Disease is in a Population at a Given Time,
# By Group rather than Raw Counts. As such, I am creating plotting functions that show how the Rate of Heart Disease Changes across
# Various Risk Factors.

target = "Heart_Disease"

# This Function focuses on Plotting a Bar Plot of Heart Disease Prevalence (%) for our Binary Features
def plot_prevalence_by_binary(df, col, target=target):
    grp = df.groupby(col)[target].mean().mul(100)  # prevalence %
    counts = df[col].value_counts().sort_index()

    plt.figure(figsize=(6,10))
    ax = grp.sort_index().plot(kind="bar")
    plt.title(f"Heart Disease Prevalence by {col}")
    plt.xlabel(f"{col}")
    plt.ylabel("Heart Disease Prevalence (%)")
    plt.xticks(rotation=0)

    for i, (p, c) in enumerate(zip(grp.sort_index().values, counts.sort_index().values)):
        ax.text(i, p + 0.1, f"{p:.1f}%\n(Number of Data Points={c})", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
In [226]:
# This Function Plots a Bar Plot for a One-Hot Encoded Group, Compute Prevalence (%) per Category.

def plot_prevalence_by_ohe_group(df, prefix, target=target, top_n=None):
    cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith(prefix)]
    if not cols:
        print(f"No columns found with prefix: {prefix}")
        return

    rows = []
    for c in cols:
        mask = df[c] == 1
        n = int(mask.sum())
        if n == 0:
            continue
        prev = df.loc[mask, target].mean() * 100
        cat = c.replace(prefix, "")
        rows.append((cat, prev, n))

    out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["category", "prevalence_pct", "n"]).sort_values("prevalence_pct", ascending=False)
    if top_n is not None:
        out = out.head(top_n)

    plt.figure(figsize=(9,8))
    ax = plt.bar(out["category"], out["prevalence_pct"])
    plt.title(f"Heart Disease Prevalence by {prefix.rstrip('_')}")
    plt.xlabel(prefix.rstrip("_"))
    plt.ylabel("Heart Disease Prevalence (%)")
    plt.xticks(rotation=0)

    # label bars
    for i, (p, n) in enumerate(zip(out["prevalence_pct"].values, out["n"].values)):
        plt.text(i, p + 0.1, f"{p:.1f}%", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    return out

def plot_numeric_distributions(df, cols, bins=30):
    for col in cols:
        plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
        plt.hist(df[col].dropna(), bins=bins)
        plt.title(f"Distribution of {col}")
        plt.xlabel(col)
        plt.ylabel("Count")

# This Function Focusses on Plotting Prevalence (%) by Quantile Bins for a Numeric Feature
def plot_prevalence_by_numeric_bins(df, col, bins=6, target=target):
    x = df[col].copy()
    # quantile bins (roughly equal-sized groups)
    qbins = pd.qcut(x, q=bins, duplicates="drop")
    grp = df.groupby(qbins)[target].mean().mul(100)
    n = df.groupby(qbins)[target].size()

    plt.figure(figsize=(10,8))
    ax = grp.plot(kind="bar")
    plt.title(f"Heart Disease Prevalence by {col} (quantile bins)")
    plt.xlabel(f"{col} bin")
    plt.ylabel("Heart Disease Prevalence (%)")
    plt.xticks(rotation=0)

    for i, (p, c) in enumerate(zip(grp.values, n.values)):

EDA #2¶

Since Heart_Disease is imbalanced, these plots use prevalence (the percent of people in each subgroup who have heart disease) rather than raw case counts. That way, we’re comparing the heart disease rate within each group. For example, “what percent of diabetics have heart disease” vs “what percent of non-diabetics have heart disease” is a much fairer and more informative comparison when the positive class is rare. Across the board, the plots show patterns that line up with established cardiovascular risk factors and comorbidity burden. Diabetes is the strongest signal in this set: the heart disease prevalence jumps from ~6.2% (no diabetes, n≈266k) to ~19.8% (diabetes, n≈43k), roughly a 3× increase. Smoking history also shows a clear elevation: ~5.7% (non-smoker, n≈184k) vs ~11.6% (smoker, n≈125k). Exercise shows a protective association in the expected direction: ~13.0% (no exercise, n≈69k) vs ~6.7% (exercise, n≈239k), about half the prevalence. Several “overall health burden” indicators are also strongly associated: arthritis (5.2% vs 14.1%), skin cancer (7.3% vs 15.6%), and other cancer (7.3% vs 15.8%) all show substantially higher heart disease prevalence among those reporting these conditions. Depression has a smaller but noticeable increase (7.6% vs 9.9%). Finally, sex shows higher prevalence for the group encoded as 1 (likely male): ~10.1% vs ~6.2%, which is directionally plausible. A key EDA takeaway is that many of these “disease status” variables are likely acting as proxies for age and overall comorbidity load (e.g., cancer and arthritis are much more common in older groups), so the apparent effect sizes here are marginal (unadjusted) and will likely change once you condition on age and other factors in modeling.

EDA #3A¶

The age plot shows a clear and expected relationship between age and heart disease: the prevalence of heart disease increases steadily as age increases. In the youngest age groups, heart disease is rare (about 0.5% for ages 18–24 and still under ~1–2% through the 30s and early 40s). Prevalence begins to rise in midlife (around ~3–5% by ages 45–54) and then increases more sharply after age 55 (about ~7% for 55–59, ~9% for 60–64, and ~11% for 65–69). The highest prevalence is observed in the oldest groups, reaching roughly ~15% for 70–74, ~18% for 75–79, and ~22% for 80+. Overall, this pattern indicates that age is likely one of the strongest predictors in the dataset and may partly explain why other conditions (such as diabetes or arthritis) appear associated with heart disease in earlier plots. No additional data cleaning is required based on this figure, but it is important to account for age in later modeling and interpretation; keeping an ordered age feature (such as an age index) can also help capture this strong monotonic trend.

EDA #3B¶

This plot compares heart disease prevalence across categories describing how recently a person had a routine checkup. The most striking pattern is that individuals who report having a checkup within the past year have the highest heart disease prevalence (about 9.5%), while all other groups fall in a lower range of roughly 2.5%–4.1% (e.g., ~4.1% for “Never,” ~3.9% for “Within the past 2 years,” ~2.7% for “Within the past 5 years,” and ~2.5% for “5 or more years ago”). This result should not be interpreted as checkups causing heart disease; instead, it likely reflects reverse causality and confounding—people with existing health conditions or higher cardiovascular risk may be more likely to visit doctors regularly, and older adults are both more likely to have heart disease and more likely to receive routine care.

These histograms below summarize the distributions of the numeric features in the dataset and highlight which variables look approximately normal versus highly skewed. BMI is right-skewed with most observations concentrated in the mid-to-high 20s and low 30s, and a long tail extending into very high values, suggesting a small number of extreme BMI observations. Height (cm) appears roughly bell-shaped and centered around typical adult heights (with most values in a plausible range), while Weight (kg) is also right-skewed with the bulk of values clustered around common adult weights and a long tail toward heavier weights. The dietary features (Fruit_Consumption, Green_Vegetables_Consumption, and FriedPotato_Consumption) are similarly skewed with strong clustering at particular values and long tails, indicating these are likely discrete frequency-style variables (e.g., times per month) rather than continuous measurements; the visible spikes suggest many respondents report common rounded amounts and a smaller number report very high consumption values.

EDA #5¶

These plots below show how heart disease prevalence changes across quantile based bins of several continuous or count like variables. For BMI, there is a clear upward trend. Heart disease prevalence increases steadily from the lowest BMI bin at about 5.8% to the highest bin at about 9.7%, indicating that higher BMI is associated with higher cardiovascular risk in this dataset. Weight in kilograms shows a very similar monotonic pattern, rising from roughly 5.9% in the lightest group to about 9.9% in the heaviest group, which is consistent with the BMI result since both capture body size and adiposity. Height in centimeters does not show a clean monotonic relationship. Prevalence varies across bins from roughly 6.4% to 9.6%, with the highest rates appearing in the middle to taller ranges, suggesting that height alone is not a strong direct risk factor and any pattern may be influenced by sex and age. For diet related variables, the relationships are weaker and less consistently monotonic. Alcohol consumption shows a non linear pattern where the lowest consumption bin has the highest prevalence at about 10.1%, mid range bins are lower at about 4.8% to 5.9%, and the highest bin rises again to about 6.8%. This likely reflects confounding, since non drinkers may include older adults or people who reduced or stopped drinking due to health issues, rather than a simple protective or harmful effect. Fruit consumption and green vegetables consumption show modest decreases in prevalence as intake increases. The highest intake groups have somewhat lower heart disease prevalence, with fruit dropping from about 9.3% to about 7.0% and green vegetables dropping from about 9.2% to as low as about 6.0% in the highest bin. This is consistent with healthier dietary patterns being associated with lower cardiovascular risk. Fried potato consumption shows a mild U shaped or weak pattern rather than a clear monotonic increase. The lowest intake group has higher prevalence at about 9.5%, the middle bins are lower at about 7.0% to 7.8%, and the highest intake bin increases again to about 7.9%, suggesting the effect is small and likely mixed with demographic confounding.

Feature Selection¶

Since our goal is to predict heart disease (a relatively rare outcome in this dataset), we cannot rely on raw accuracy or on simple visual inspection alone when deciding which variables to keep for modeling. With an imbalanced target, a model can appear to perform well by mostly predicting the majority class, and noisy or redundant features can easily reduce the model’s ability to detect the minority class. Feature selection addresses this by identifying the variables that carry the most useful information about the outcome, improving model stability, reducing overfitting, and producing a simpler and more interpretable final model. In this project, feature selection is especially important because we have a mix of binary features (e.g., smoking history, diabetes), ordinal-like survey responses (e.g., general health, checkup recency, age categories), and continuous variables (e.g., BMI, weight, diet frequencies), many of which are correlated or may partially capture the same underlying health status.

As a result, we will be using a two stage feature selection approach to balance interpretability with predictive relevance. In the first stage, we apply a filter method using mutual information to rank features by how informative they are about the heart disease outcome. Mutual information is well suited here because it can capture both linear and non linear relationships and can be applied across mixed feature types. This stage provides an initial screening step that helps remove clearly uninformative variables and produces a ranked list that can be compared back to our EDA findings. Importantly, this ranking is computed only on the training data, which prevents information leakage from the test set and ensures that later evaluation remains a fair estimate of generalization.

In the second stage, we perform embedded feature selection using L1 regularized logistic regression. Unlike filter methods that score each feature independently, L1 regularization selects features while fitting a predictive model, allowing it to account for redundancy and correlation among variables. The L1 penalty encourages sparsity by shrinking weak or redundant feature coefficients to exactly zero, leaving a compact subset of predictors that best support the classification task. Because the dataset is imbalanced, we incorporate class weighting so the training process places additional emphasis on correctly learning patterns for the minority heart disease class. We tune the amount of regularization using stratified cross validation and evaluate performance using PR AUC, which is more informative than accuracy for rare outcomes. Together, these two stages produce a feature set that is both defensible from an exploratory standpoint and optimized for predictive performance, while keeping the modeling pipeline transparent and reproducible.

# This cell performs embedded feature selection using L1-regularized Logistic Regression.
# We use class_weight='balanced' to account for the imbalanced target and tune C via CV.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, GridSearchCV

logreg_l1 = LogisticRegression(
    penalty="l1",
    solver="saga",
    max_iter=5000,
    class_weight="balanced",
    n_jobs=-1
)

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scaler", StandardScaler(with_mean=False)),  # safe if any sparse-like structure; works fine for dense too
    ("clf", logreg_l1)
])

param_grid = {
    "clf__C": np.logspace(-3, 1, 9)  # 0.001 to 10
}

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

# Use average precision (PR AUC) which is more informative than accuracy for imbalance
grid = GridSearchCV(
    pipe, param_grid=param_grid,
    scoring="average_precision",
    cv=cv, n_jobs=-1, verbose=1
)

grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Best PR AUC (CV):", grid.best_score_)
print("Best C:", grid.best_params_["clf__C"])

best_model = grid.best_estimator_
coef = best_model.named_steps["clf"].coef_.ravel()

selected_features = X_train.columns[coef != 0]
print("Selected feature count:", len(selected_features))
selected_features[:30]

Now, let me explain the results of our feature selection. We first computed a Mutual Information (MI) ranking, which is a simple one feature at a time measure of how informative each feature is about the target variable(Heart_Disease) on its own. That is why variables like Diabetes, Arthritis, Age_Category, General_Health, and Smoking_History appear near the top, because each one individually carries a strong signal. However, MI does not account for redundancy, meaning it can rank several highly related features as “important” even if they are basically telling the model the same thing. For example, BMI and weight related measures overlap substantially, and multiple age buckets are closely related, so MI alone can over emphasize groups of correlated predictors.

Next, we performed cross validated feature selection using a regularized Logistic Regression model while tuning the regularization strength (C). The output showing “Fitting 5 folds…” and “Best C: 0.01… Selected feature count…”, which indicates that the model is selecting features in a multivariate way, meaning it chooses predictors that still add value after the other predictors are already included. This step is important because it naturally removes redundant or weak features and keeps only the set that contributes unique predictive information. That also explains why some variables that look decent under MI (especially diet variables) may be dropped if their relationship with heart disease is largely explained by stronger drivers like age, diabetes status, BMI, and general health.

Finally, the evaluation metrics reinforce why we treat this as an imbalanced classification problem. A Test ROC AUC around 0.83 suggests the model does a good job ranking higher risk individuals above lower risk individuals overall. Meanwhile, the Test PR AUC around 0.31 looks smaller because precision recall performance is much harder when the positive class is rare (around 8 percent in your dataset), and PR AUC is designed to reflect that difficulty more honestly. For the feature list we use moving forward, the most defensible choice is the cross validated, regularization based selected feature set, because it has already been tuned to reduce redundancy and noise and therefore provides a cleaner, more stable input for training the downstream models.

Model Training and Testing¶

In this section, we create a small set of reusable functions that standardize how we train, tune, and evaluate every model in our tutorial. We do this because once we move beyond a single baseline model, the workflow becomes repetitive: each algorithm needs cross validation, hyperparameter tuning, probability based evaluation, threshold selection, and a final test set report. If we copy and paste that logic separately for Logistic Regression, k Nearest Neighbors, and Random Forest, we increase the risk of mistakes, inconsistency, and “apples to oranges” comparisons. By wrapping the common steps into functions, we ensure that every model is trained under the same evaluation protocol and that any future model we add later can plug into the same pipeline with minimal changes. This also makes the notebook easier to follow for a reader, because the modeling logic stays clean and the details of cross validation and metrics are handled in a consistent way.

Our helper functions are designed specifically for the challenges of predicting heart disease in an imbalanced dataset, where the positive class is relatively rare and false negatives are costly. Instead of only reporting accuracy, we focus on probability based metrics like PR AUC (average precision) and ROC AUC, and we explicitly tune the decision threshold to improve recall when needed. The key idea is that a classifier does not just output labels, it outputs probabilities, and we can choose the probability cutoff that best matches our goal. To avoid overfitting, we tune thresholds using out of fold predictions from the training set (OOF probabilities), which lets us “practice” threshold selection without ever looking at the test set. Then we lock that threshold in and evaluate once on the test set for a fair final report.

First, we define the run_gridsearch function that runs GridSearchCV using stratified cross validation, meaning each fold preserves the same class balance as the full dataset. We do this because our target is imbalanced, so we cannot rely on random splits that might accidentally produce folds with too few positive examples. We also choose PR AUC (average precision) as the default scoring metric, since it is more informative than accuracy when positives are rare. The purpose of this function is to make sure we tune every model the same way: we search a grid of hyperparameters, identify the best setting based on cross validated performance, and return a fitted estimator that we can evaluate consistently.

Our Next function, threshold_table, evaluates many probability thresholds and creates a table of performance metrics at each threshold. We do this because the default threshold of 0.5 is rarely optimal for imbalanced classification, especially when we care about reducing false negatives. For each threshold, we compute the confusion matrix components (true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives) and also compute precision, recall, F1, and F beta. We include F beta because it lets us deliberately weight recall more heavily than precision when false negatives matter more than false positives. This table becomes a clear way to see the tradeoff: as we lower the threshold, recall usually increases but precision often decreases, and the table makes that decision transparent.

After that, we define a function called pick_threshold that selects the best threshold according to a rule. We support two practical strategies. The first strategy chooses the threshold that maximizes F beta, which is useful when we want a single balanced objective but still want recall emphasized (for example, beta=2 weighs recall more than precision). The second strategy enforces a minimum recall requirement and then selects the threshold that gives the best precision while meeting that recall target. We include both because different applications call for different priorities. In our problem, missing a heart disease case can be more costly than issuing a false alarm, so we need the ability to intentionally prefer thresholds that reduce false negatives.

Then we define oof_proba, a function that generates out of fold predicted probabilities on the training set. We do this because threshold selection can itself overfit if we repeatedly adjust thresholds based on test set results. Out of fold predictions solve this problem by generating probabilities for each training point from a model that was not trained on that point (because it came from a different fold). This gives us a realistic “training only” probability distribution that mimics test time behavior, so we can choose thresholds honestly. In short, we tune the threshold using training data only, and we reserve the test set for a single final evaluation.

Finally, we define the evaluate_with_threshold function that fits the final model on the full training set, predicts probabilities on the test set, applies the chosen threshold, and then prints key metrics and a confusion matrix. We use this function to keep the evaluation consistent across models: every model reports ROC AUC and PR AUC (probability quality) as well as precision, recall, and F1 at the chosen threshold (decision quality). We also visualize the confusion matrix because it makes false negatives and false positives immediately clear. This is especially important for our tutorial because the reader can see exactly how many cases the model is missing, not just a single summary score.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, GridSearchCV, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import (
    confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay,
    precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, fbeta_score,
    roc_auc_score, average_precision_score
)

def run_gridsearch(estimator, param_grid, X_train, y_train,
                   scoring="average_precision", n_splits=5, random_state=42,
                   n_jobs=-1, verbose=1):
    """
    Fits GridSearchCV and returns the fitted grid object.
    scoring='average_precision' (PR AUC) is usually a solid choice for imbalanced targets.
    """
    cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)
    grid = GridSearchCV(
        estimator=estimator,
        param_grid=param_grid,
        scoring=scoring,
        cv=cv,
        n_jobs=n_jobs,
        verbose=verbose,
        refit=True
    )
    grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
    return grid

def threshold_table(y_true, y_proba, thresholds=None, beta=2):
    """
    Creates a table of metrics by threshold. beta>1 emphasizes recall (reducing FN).
    """
    if thresholds is None:
        thresholds = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)

    rows = []
    for t in thresholds:
        y_pred = (y_proba >= t).astype(int)
        tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()

        prec = precision_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0)
        rec  = recall_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0)
        f1   = f1_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0)
        fB   = fbeta_score(y_true, y_pred, beta=beta, zero_division=0)

        rows.append({
            "threshold": float(t),
            "precision": prec,
            "recall": rec,
            "f1": f1,
            f"f{beta}": fB,
            "tn": tn, "fp": fp, "fn": fn, "tp": tp
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("threshold").reset_index(drop=True)

def pick_threshold(thr_df, mode="max_fbeta", beta=2, min_recall=0.80):
    """
    mode:
      - 'max_fbeta'   : picks threshold maximizing F-beta (beta>1 reduces FN)
      - 'min_recall'  : picks highest-precision threshold among those with recall >= min_recall
    """
    if mode == "max_fbeta":
        col = f"f{beta}"
        best = thr_df.loc[thr_df[col].idxmax()]
        return float(best["threshold"]), best

    if mode == "min_recall":
        cand = thr_df[thr_df["recall"] >= min_recall].copy()
        if cand.empty:
            return None, None
        best = cand.loc[cand["precision"].idxmax()]
        return float(best["threshold"]), best

    raise ValueError("mode must be 'max_fbeta' or 'min_recall'")

def oof_proba(estimator, X_train, y_train, n_splits=5, random_state=42):
    """
    Out-of-fold probabilities for threshold tuning (train-only).
    """
    cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)
    proba = cross_val_predict(estimator, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, method="predict_proba", n_jobs=-1)[:, 1]
    return proba

def evaluate_with_threshold(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, threshold, title="Model"):
    """
    Fit on full train, evaluate once on test using the chosen threshold.
    """
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    test_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    test_pred = (test_proba >= threshold).astype(int)

    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, test_pred).ravel()

    print(f"\n{title} (threshold={threshold:.2f})")
    print("TN, FP, FN, TP:", tn, fp, fn, tp)
    print("Test ROC AUC:", roc_auc_score(y_test, test_proba))
    print("Test PR  AUC:", average_precision_score(y_test, test_proba))
    print("Precision :", precision_score(y_test, test_pred, zero_division=0))
    print("Recall    :", recall_score(y_test, test_pred, zero_division=0))
    print("F1        :", f1_score(y_test, test_pred, zero_division=0))

    disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=confusion_matrix(y_test, test_pred))
    disp.plot(values_format="d")
    plt.title(f"{title} Confusion Matrix (threshold={threshold:.2f})")
    plt.show()

    return {"threshold": threshold, "tn": tn, "fp": fp, "fn": fn, "tp": tp}

# 1) Separate target and features
target_col = "Heart_Disease"
y = df[target_col].astype(int)
X = df.drop(columns=[target_col])

# 2) Stratified split to preserve the rare positive-class rate in both splits
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=99,
    stratify=y

For Logistic Regression, we use a pipeline that includes StandardScaler followed by the classifier. We do this because logistic regression is sensitive to feature scale, and our dataset includes continuous variables like BMI, height, weight, and consumption measures whose ranges differ significantly. Scaling ensures that features contribute more comparably during optimization and helps the solver converge reliably. We then tune the regularization strength C, which controls how flexible the model is, and we tune whether we apply class weighting (class_weight="balanced"). Class weighting is important here because it increases the penalty for misclassifying the minority class, which often improves recall and reduces false negatives.

After finding the best hyperparameters using GridSearchCV, we use out of fold probabilities to select a threshold that better matches our goal. Because our positive class is rare and false negatives are a concern, we often prefer a threshold that maximizes F2 or meets a recall constraint. Finally, we evaluate on the test set once with that fixed threshold. This gives us a clean, interpretable baseline model that is easy to explain and also provides probability outputs for threshold tuning.

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

lr_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=42))
])

lr_param_grid = {
    "clf__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10],
    "clf__penalty": ["l2"],
    "clf__solver": ["lbfgs"],
    "clf__class_weight": [None, "balanced"]   # helps reduce FN
}

lr_grid = run_gridsearch(
    lr_pipe, lr_param_grid, X_train, y_train,
    scoring="average_precision",  # PR AUC for imbalanced
    verbose=1
)

print("LR best params:", lr_grid.best_params_)
print("LR best CV PR AUC:", lr_grid.best_score_)

# Threshold tuning on TRAIN only using OOF probabilities
lr_oof = oof_proba(lr_grid.best_estimator_, X_train, y_train)
lr_thr_df = threshold_table(y_train, lr_oof, beta=2)

# Pick threshold to reduce FN:
# Option 1: maximize F2 (more recall emphasis than F1)
lr_t, lr_row = pick_threshold(lr_thr_df, mode="max_fbeta", beta=2)
# Option 2 (stricter): require recall >= 0.80 and maximize precision among those
# lr_t, lr_row = pick_threshold(lr_thr_df, mode="min_recall", min_recall=0.80, beta=2)

print("Chosen LR threshold + OOF metrics:\n", lr_row)

# Final: evaluate ONCE on test
lr_results = evaluate_with_threshold(
    lr_grid.best_estimator_, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test,
    threshold=lr_t,
    title="Logistic Regression (GridSearch + OOF threshold)"
)

For k Nearest Neighbors, we again use a scaling pipeline, because kNN relies on distance computations. Without scaling, one feature with a large numeric range could dominate distance and distort neighborhoods, leading to unstable or misleading predictions. We tune the number of neighbors n_neighbors because it controls the bias variance tradeoff: smaller k makes the classifier more sensitive to local patterns but noisier, while larger k smooths predictions but may miss important minority class structure. We also tune the weighting strategy (uniform vs distance), since distance weighting can help when closer neighbors should matter more than farther ones. Finally, we tune the Minkowski distance parameter p, which lets us compare Manhattan like behavior (p=1) versus Euclidean like behavior (p=2).

Because kNN produces probabilities based on neighbor voting, we can apply the same threshold tuning strategy as with logistic regression. We again select the threshold using out of fold probabilities from the training set, so we reduce false negatives without leaking information from the test set. This is especially important for kNN because probability calibration can vary depending on k and weighting, and threshold selection helps adapt the final decision boundary to our risk focused goal.

For Random Forest, we do not scale features because tree based models are not sensitive to feature magnitude in the same way linear and distance based models are. Instead, we focus on tuning parameters that control model complexity and generalization. We tune n_estimators to ensure enough trees for stable performance, max_depth to prevent overly complex trees that overfit, and min_samples_leaf to enforce a minimum number of samples in each leaf, which smooths the model and reduces variance. We also tune class_weight because Random Forest can still be biased toward the majority class in imbalanced settings, and class weighting encourages the model to pay more attention to positive examples.

After selecting the best hyperparameters using cross validation and PR AUC, we again use out of fold probabilities to tune the classification threshold. This is helpful because even if the forest ranks risk well, the default probability cutoff may not align with our objective of reducing false negatives. Using the same threshold tuning approach across models also makes our comparisons fair: each model is evaluated under a decision rule that is optimized using training only information and then tested once on the holdout set.

Interpretation of our Results¶

Across all three models, we intentionally used a low decision threshold of 0.10 (picked from out of fold predictions) to reduce false negatives, since missing a true heart disease case is the costliest error in a screening style setting. This choice shifts the models toward higher sensitivity (recall), but it also increases false positives, meaning more people get flagged for follow up even if they are actually negative. That trade off is expected and it is exactly what we want when the goal is to catch as many true positives as possible.

On the held out test set, the Logistic Regression model gives the strongest overall performance and the best balance for our goal. It achieves a ROC AUC of about 0.822 and a PR AUC of about 0.274, with recall around 0.672 and precision around 0.217 at the 0.10 threshold. In confusion matrix terms, it correctly identifies 168 true positives while missing 82 positives (false negatives), and it produces 606 false positives. Random Forest and kNN end up with very similar recall (both about 0.68) and very similar confusion matrices (both correctly find 170 true positives and miss 80 false negatives), but they do so with more false positives (658 for Random Forest, 661 for kNN) and lower ranking performance overall (Random Forest ROC AUC about 0.814 and PR AUC about 0.254, kNN ROC AUC about 0.792 and PR AUC about 0.243). So, if we want the best “catch positives without exploding false alarms” setup, Logistic Regression is our current best model, while Random Forest and kNN are close in recall but slightly worse in precision and PR AUC under the same thresholding strategy.
